blocks.text: i: DNA Cleavage: The source DNA of the organisms is cleaved by using a restriction endonuclease and the gene of interest is isolated. Similarly, the DNA of vector (e.g., plasmid or viral DNA) is also cleaved by using the same endonuclease. So, compatible sticky ends are produced at the gene of interest and the cleaved vector.

blocks.alt: Four steps. Step 1: DNA from an animal cell, with restriction endonuclease recognition sites around the gene of interest, and a plasmid from E. coli (lacZ' gene with a recognition site, antibiotic resistance gene) are cut with the same enzyme, giving sticky ends. Step 2: DNA ligase joins them into recombinant DNA plasmids with a nonfunctional lacZ' gene. Step 3: the plasmids enter bacterial cells, which form Clones 1, 2 and 3. Step 4: clones are screened for the gene of interest.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.3: Steps of making Recombinant Vectors (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.3).
blocks.long_description: Step texts: Step 1: DNA from 2 sources is isolated and cleaved with the same restriction endonuclease. Step 2: DNA ligase joins the 2 types of DNA at their sticky ends. Step 3: Recombinant DNA is inserted into bacterial cells, which reproduce and form clones. Step 4: Clones are screened for gene of interest. Other labels: Animal cell, DNA, Gene of interest, E. coli, Plasmid, lacZ' gene, Recognition site, Antibiotic resistance gene, Sticky ends, Recombinant DNA, Nonfunctional lacZ' gene, Clone 1, Clone 2, Clone 3.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 20.3 labels the plasmid gene 'Antibody resistance gene'; it is an antibiotic resistance gene, as drawn above.

ii: Production of Recombinant DNA (Vector): The gene of interest is inserted into the cleaved vector. For this purpose, the cleaved vector and the gene of interest are incubated together in the presence of DNA ligase. This enzyme connects them by forming phosphodiester linkages. So, the vector turns into recombinant vector (i.e., vector having the gene of interest).

The recombinant DNA (vector) and the expression system (usually bacteria) are incubated in the same medium. The bacterial cells take up recombinant DNA. All the incubated bacteria make bacterial clones which also contain the identical copies i.e., clones of the gene of interest.
Once the vectors have been inserted into host cells, scientists identify which bacteria actually took up the recombinant plasmid. This is done through:

i: Selecting for the Vector (Antibiotic Resistance): The plasmid contains an antibiotic resistance gene. The bacteria are grown on a medium containing that antibiotic (e.g., ampicillin). Only cells that took up a plasmid will survive and grow.

ii: Selecting for the Gene of Interest (Blue-White Screening): To distinguish between a "plain" plasmid and a "recombinant plasmid", the lacZ' gene of the plasmid is used. The lacZ' gene produces an enzyme which metabolizes a specific sugar and turns it blue.

blocks.alt: Four kinds of bacterial cell: plasmid with functional lacZ' gene; no plasmid; plasmid with gene of interest; plasmid with DNA fragment (non-functional lacZ' gene). An arrow 'Eliminate cells without plasmid' leads to a plate with antibiotic in media, where only cells with a plasmid make clones. An arrow 'Eliminate cells without rDNA' leads to a plate with sugar in media: blue clones without rDNA and white clones with rDNA.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.4: Screening of clones (Elimination of clones without vector (plasmid) and elimination of clones with vector (plasmid) but without recombinant DNA) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.4).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Plasmid with functional lacZ' gene, No plasmid, Plasmid with gene of interest, Plasmid with DNA fragment, Non-functional lacZ' gene, Eliminate cells without plasmid, Antibiotic in media, Clones with plasmid, Cells without plasmid did not make clone, Eliminate cells without rDNA, Sugar in media, Clones with rDNA, Clones without rDNA (have functional lacZ' gene and metabolize sugar).

blocks.text: If the plasmid is not recombinant, the lacZ' gene remains functional and turns the bacterial colony blue. If gene of interest was successfully inserted, it "breaks" the lacZ' gene. Therefore, the desired recombinant clones will remain white.

iii: Identifying the Specific Gene (DNA Hybridization): To confirm the presence of gene of interest, a radioactive probe is used. It is a DNA strand complementary to gene of interest. The probe sticks (hybridizes) only to the colonies containing the gene of interest. Auto-radiography (photographic film) is used to locate these specific colonies on the master plate. The main steps of this technique are mentioned in the following diagram.

blocks.alt: Five numbered steps around three drawings. 1: clones of bacteria with plasmid grown on an agar plate. 2: a filter is pressed on the clones to make a replica. 3: the filter is washed with a DNA-denaturing solution containing a radioactive probe. 4: a film placed over the filter shows a spot only where clones keep the probe. 5: an arrow from the spot back to the original plate identifies the clone with the gene of interest.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.5: Identification of the clones that have gene of interest (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.5).
blocks.long_description: Step texts: 1 Clones of bacteria, which have plasmid, are grown on agar. 2 A replica of plate is made by pressing a filter against the clones. Some cells from each clone attach with the filter. 3 The filter is washed with a solution that denatures DNA. The solution has radioactively-labelled probe (nucleotide sequence complementary to gene of interest). The probe binds to the cells which contain gene of interest. 4 Only those clones which contain gene of interest retain the probe and emit radioactivity on film placed over the filter. 5 A comparison with the original plate identifies the clone containing the gene of interest. Labels: Filter, Film.
